sources.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
sources.text: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang poured money into open-source AI, from French-founded Hugging Face to chips for Mistral's data centres, and fought Washington's attempts to restrict it. With Huang gone and China hawks emboldened, Tech 24 asks whether Europe's AI ambitions have lost their most powerful ally, and whether he was ever the champion Europe needed.

sources.headline: Megaspeed says alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, left company last year
sources.text:
By Hugo Murphy
Published on
15 November 2026 - 17:41 GMT+1
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, accused of spying for China and linked to an alleged affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, left the Singapore-based data center company in August 2025.
The company, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, is currently conducting an internal probe over the scandal.
US intelligence authorities suspect that Alice Huang had links to China's Ministry of State Security and may have been recruited as an intelligence asset.
Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs has, however, explicitly stated that Alice Huang was not investigated for espionage. In a statement published on November 12, the ministry said that the investigation into Huang concerned suspected offences relating to the purchase and export of servers, and not alleged links to Chinese intelligence.
The ex-Nvidia CEO is alleged to have had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang. On November 8, Jensen Huang admitted having an affair although Ms. Huang is not mentioned by name. Nvidia, the American multinational tech company, has lost nearly $2tn in value since the story became public, although a direct link remains unclear.
According to a statement published by Megaspeed, Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company”. Ms. Huang had been serving as the controlling shareholder of the company since March 2023.
Singaporean authorities are continuing their investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals, while the company is also under scrutiny in the US over alleged export control violations.
According to media reports, Megaspeed is alleged to have supplied high-end AI chips to China through a network of shell companies and false declarations. The allegations have not been proven, and Singaporean authorities are continuing their investigation.
Nvidia had been working with Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce giant. Ms. Huang is said to have deepened commercial ties between Nvidia and Alibaba.
Nvidia has defended its commercial operations. In a statement published last week, the company’s board stated it had no reason to believe that US national security or confidential Nvidia trade secrets were compromised.
Huang, a former journalist for Chinese state media, worked at HSBC Hong Kong and CITIC Securities and Hexi Capital where she met her husband Kang Wei. Mr. Wei later introduced Huang to the former Nvidia CEO. Jensen Huang is accused of taking part in further extra-marital affairs.

sources.headline: Alleged Chinese spy left Megaspeed last year, company says
sources.text: Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International says Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang sparked US national security concerns, left the company last year.Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.The company said it ran a "legitimate and lawful business" and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations "that are not supported by verifiable evidence".It did not address specific allegations."The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," it said in an emailed statement.Jensen Huang (centre) admitted to having an affair with Megaspeed's Alice Huang. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)Alice Huang "left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company," the statement said."Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang's personal and private matters."A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from US authorities, over allegations that it circumvented US export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies.Last December, it said there was "no evidence" of illicit chip transfers.Singapore's government said last week it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible "false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers".Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed's then-chief executive, chairperson and one of its key controllers.Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided "inaccurate" information to downplay her role at the company.An earlier New York Times report suggested US officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced on Thursday that he was stepping down as chief executive.Nvidia's chips are widely used to develop AI models. (Reuters: Ann Wang)US Attorney General Todd Blanche said, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: "I don't know if that's been determined yet."Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International.It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.The company's finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from the end of 2023 to 2024, reaching almost $US3 billion ($4.4 billion).AP

sources.headline: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in 2025, denies wrongdoing
sources.text:
By
Updated on: November 15, 2026 / 2:10 PM EST
/ CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
The Singapore-based company at the center of the scandal that brought down Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Sunday that suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang left the company in 2025. It also denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."In a statement to CBS News, Megaspeed International said Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, left the company in August 2025 and has no current role. It did not comment on the allegations that Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy."Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed and is the woman with whom Jensen Huang was having an affair. She is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week.U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China.
A screengrab from CTI video footage shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, in black, at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, May 22, 2025.
CTI via Reuters TV
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.Now the company, which began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to the Nvidia chips, is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips into China. In a statement to CBS News on Sunday, the company said that recent assertions about its business, supply chain and global operations are "not supported by verifiable evidence."
"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.It added: "The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation."
The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026.
Taryn NG /AFP via Getty Images
President Trump said last week the FBI was investigating the romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related.CBS News reported on Friday that Singaporean authorities seized Alice Huang's passport in June 2025 while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into the suspected smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The source added that the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington at the time.

Published: 10:22pm, 9 Nov 2026Updated: 1:35pm, 12 Nov 2026
A little-known Singapore-registered company is embroiled in a mounting love scandal surrounding Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and US allegations of Chinese espionage.

Huang’s admission of an extramarital affair has renewed scrutiny of Megaspeed, after media reports identified a former executive of the Singapore firm as the woman involved in the relationship, which US officials suspect was linked to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, is believed to have been founded and led by Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, the woman identified in the media reports and accused of spying for Beijing.

Jensen Huang did not name the woman in his admission, while China’s foreign ministry has dismissed the espionage allegation as “groundless”.

The company occupies a unit on the seventh floor of a sleek office building in Singapore’s central business district, but This Week in Asia was denied access during a site visit on Monday.

Local media outlet The Straits Times reported last year that no activity or occupants were seen in the unit.

Megaspeed, which has reportedly bought billions of dollars’ worth of chips from US tech giant Nvidia for its data centres, is under investigation by US authorities over allegations that it helped Chinese firms circumvent American export restrictions on advanced AI chips.

Megaspeed’s total assets surged almost 90-fold from US$32.9 million in 2023 to US$2.98 billion in 2024, according to Singapore’s business registry. Its assets were valued at just US$75 in 2022.

The firm’s revenue rose from almost zero in 2023 to US$294 million in 2024. Its total liabilities jumped from US$22.9 million to nearly US$3 billion during the same period. The company had US$20,300 in liabilities in 2022.

Megaspeed’s financial statement for 2025 has not been publicly disclosed.

Alice Huang (right), a Chinese executive linked to the data centre company called Megaspeed, attends a dinner hosted by Nvidia chief Jensen Huang (left) at a restaurant in Taipei on May 22, 2025. Photo: CTI via AFPTV / AFP

Singapore separately confirmed in October 2025 that it was investigating Megaspeed for suspected breaches of domestic law, without specifying the alleged offences. Police said on October 30 this year that the investigation remained ongoing. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

Singaporean Tan Yong Pong has been the firm’s director since November 2023, the same month Chinese national Huang Le ended an eight-month tenure as managing director, according to Singapore’s business registry. Huang Le is Alice Huang’s Chinese name.

The company – first registered in Singapore in 2015 – was previously called 7Road International, which is also the name of a Shenzhen-based gaming firm.

The Singapore company changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023, the same month Huang Le assumed her position there.

Megaspeed’s sole registered shareholder is Swiftdata, which records show was incorporated in October 2023 and is owned by Tan. Under Singapore law, all local companies must keep accurate records of key persons, including directors and shareholders.

Despite confirming investigations into Megaspeed, Singapore has denied investigating Alice Huang’s ties to China. The home affairs ministry on October 31 refuted a Wall Street Journal article which cited sources stating that the city state had investigated the businesswoman’s ties to China.

“We would like to make clear that neither the Singapore government nor its officials said this. And there were no such investigations conducted in respect of Alice Huang,” said Singapore’s home affairs ministry, after the article was published.

Singapore did not implement unilateral export controls imposed by foreign jurisdictions, police said on October 30 in response to a query from the news outlet.

“At the same time, Singapore does not condone businesses deliberately using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries’ export controls.”

As a company incorporated in Singapore, Megaspeed was legally required to retain records of the sale and purchase of AI chips for five years, said Low Yiyang, director at law firm Silvester Legal.

The city state’s Strategic Goods (Control) Act typically required a permit to import or export strategic goods, which could include certain AI chips, he said, adding that companies risked breaching the law if such goods were traded without the necessary permits, or if end-use declarations and undertakings submitted to secure them were later found to be fraudulent.

This Week in Asia has contacted Megaspeed, 7Road and the Singapore Police Force for comment.

People walk past the Nvidia logo sign displayed outside the corporation’s headquarters in Taipei, Taiwan, on Monday. Photo: EPA

According to its website, Megaspeed is an Nvidia cloud partner and “core business partner” of the US firm’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region, and operates data centres in “East South Asia”. It has two to 10 employees, and offices in Jakarta and Johor, Malaysia, according to its LinkedIn page.

Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, bought at least US$4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February, according to records cited by The New York Times. US officials reportedly visited Megaspeed’s data centre in Malaysia to investigate suspicions about how much it was buying.

In December last year, Megaspeed refuted a Bloomberg report alleging illegal chip transfers, saying the company had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by Nvidia and the US and Malaysian governments.

The investigations confirmed there was “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities” and showed the firm was “compliant and legitimate”, Megaspeed said.

Megaspeed reshared the statement on its LinkedIn account on Monday, a day after Jensen Huang admitted his infidelity and apologised in a memo to Nvidia’s employees. He did not disclose the name of the woman.

The same day, the tech giant said in a statement that the board was initiating an independent investigation into Jensen Huang being the target of a “foreign intelligence effort”, but noted it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”.

Nvidia said Jensen Huang “fully supports” and was committed to cooperating with the review.

In an interview filmed less than a month ago, Jensen Huang told Bloomberg that the firm had checked all of Megaspeed’s chip deployments to ensure that no illegal shipments to China were made.

He said that his relationship and interactions with Alice Huang – who is “no longer with Megaspeed” – were related to the Singapore-based company and were “all completely normal and not unusual”.

Kolette Lim

Kolette Lim joined the Post’s Asia desk as a reporter in 2025, and writes about a wide range of topics concerning Singapore and the region. She graduated from Nanyang Technological University with a degree in Communication Studies and a second major in Business. She previously wrote for The Straits Times, where she covered breaking news.
